investigation.title: React Dropzone Library Comparison
investigation.description: A comparison of the top 4 MIT-licensed React file drop libraries, evaluated for developer experience, UI quality, bundle size, and feature set. Each library was tested with .csv/.zip file restrictions and a 10 MB size limit.

constraints_tested.notes: Windows browsers report .zip as application/x-zip-compressed — all implementations account for this

libraries.name: react-dropzone
libraries.description: Simple HTML5 drag-and-drop zone for React. Lightweight, hooks-based, and zero dependencies. The most widely adopted dropzone library in the React ecosystem.

implementation.styling_approach: Pure styled-components — full control, no CSS overrides needed

pros: By far the most popular — huge community and examples
Clean hooks API (useDropzone) — easy to compose
Full control over UI — renders nothing itself
cons: No built-in upload progress or server communication
No image preview out of the box
libraries.best_for: Projects that need a simple, highly customisable drop target with minimal overhead

libraries.name: @uppy/react + @uppy/core
libraries.description: Modular, extensible file uploader from Transloadit. Plugin-based architecture supports resumable uploads (Tus), cloud sources (Google Drive, Dropbox), image editing, and more. Most feature-rich option.

implementation.rejection_approach: useUppyEvent(uppy, 'restriction-failed', (file, error) => ...) — must be inside UppyContextProvider
implementation.styling_approach: useDropzone hook returns getRootProps/getInputProps — wrap in styled div
important_notes: @uppy/drag-drop is deprecated in Uppy v5 — do not install
useUppyEvent and useDropzone must be called inside a child of UppyContextProvider
Set autoProceed: false when no real server is configured

pros: Most starred (30K+) — very well maintained by Transloadit
Huge plugin ecosystem (Tus, S3, Google Drive, Dropbox, Webcam, etc.)
Built-in upload progress, retry, and error handling
Supports resumable uploads via Tus protocol
Headless React hooks in v5 — clean integration
cons: Larger bundle (~25 kB gzipped for core + react)
More complex setup — requires UppyContextProvider pattern
Plugin-based architecture has a learning curve
libraries.best_for: Projects needing production-grade uploads — resumable, cloud sources, progress tracking, or S3/Transloadit integration

libraries.name: react-filepond + filepond
libraries.description: Feature-rich file upload widget with a polished built-in UI. Supports image preview, encoding, EXIF orientation, and an extensive plugin ecosystem. Renders its own UI so less custom styling needed.

implementation.package_install: npm install filepond react-filepond filepond-plugin-file-validate-type filepond-plugin-file-validate-size
implementation.rejection_approach: onaddfile(error, file) — error is non-null (FilePondErrorDescription with .body) on rejection
implementation.styling_approach: Import filepond/dist/filepond.min.css globally, override .filepond--* classes in a scoped wrapper
important_notes: registerPlugin() must be called before the component is used — call at module level
Validation plugins (file-validate-type, file-validate-size) are separate npm packages
CSS must be imported — best done in main.tsx for global scope

pros: Beautiful built-in UI — polished drop zone with file list, progress, and thumbnails
Extensive plugin ecosystem (image preview, crop, EXIF, encode, etc.)
Handles chunked and server uploads well
cons: Requires CSS import — harder to fully theme to a custom design system
Component-based (not hooks) — less composable than react-dropzone or Uppy v5
Overriding built-in styles requires specificity tricks
Larger footprint when validation plugins are added
libraries.best_for: Projects where you want a polished out-of-the-box UI with minimal custom styling, especially with image uploads

libraries.name: @rpldy/uploady
libraries.description: Modern context-based upload framework for React. Highly composable via hooks — you build the UI entirely yourself using provided primitives. Unique in supporting both file and text-based uploads.

implementation.type_filter_approach: fileFilter prop on <Uploady> — (file: File | string) => boolean
implementation.rejection_approach: No native rejection event — use dropHandler on UploadDropZone to inspect raw DragEvent files and diff against fileFilter logic
implementation.styling_approach: Pure styled-components — UploadDropZone renders a div, use extraProps for drag event callbacks
important_notes: destination prop is required on <Uploady> even for demo purposes
Set autoUpload: false when no real server
UploadDropZone does not expose onDragOver/onDragLeave props — use extraProps to pass them
dropHandler receives raw DragEvent — use e.dataTransfer.files to access all dropped files including rejected ones

pros: Pure styled-components friendly — no CSS to fight
Good for building completely custom upload UIs
cons: Smallest community (~1.9K stars) — fewer examples and Stack Overflow answers
No native rejection feedback — requires workaround via dropHandler
UploadDropZone doesn't expose drag callbacks directly
destination prop required even when not uploading
libraries.best_for: Projects needing a fully custom upload UI with composable hooks, especially where chunked uploads or custom server protocols are required
